Photograph: Benoît Tessier/Reuters Trump administration ‘Nakedly political’: US attempts to link trans support to authoritarianism in new HHS report HHS releases report linking ‘gender ideology’ to political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted Melody Schreiber Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 07.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) recently released a report linking “gender ideology” to leftwing authoritarianism and political violence – a study scientists say was poorly conducted and “nakedly political”, likely leading to greater politicization of science and health. It follows attempts by the administration to limit access to gender-affirming care – including, on Friday, an agreement reached between the Department of Justice and a New York hospital to no longer offer pediatric gender-affirming care. Dozens of hospitals stopped offering gender-affirming care after the Trump administration began investigating them for offering the standard of care. Patients on Medicaid and government insurance plans have also been blocked from accessing care, and a proposed rule would block any health system offering gender-affirming care from receiving federal funding. The new report, which was not published by a scientific journal and did not undergo peer review, takes aim at medical organizations offering guidelines on gender-affirming care. It also links those who say they support trans individuals with supporting authoritarianism and political violence. Even in safe-haven Massachusetts, trans care is at risk. Young people are fighting to protect it Read more “It was a very poorly done piece of research,” said Gideon Meyerowitz-Katz, an epidemiologist from the University of Sydney, who highlighted several methodological failings. “It was nakedly political. I think this is probably the most obviously political study that I’ve come across.” The report is “quite an abnormal document with a number of oddities,” said Daniel Aaron, an associate professor at the University of Utah’s SJ Quinney College of Law. “It likely also violates federal law because it’s not peer-reviewed, and it’s essentially quite an influential dissemination of information,” which could mean it violates the Information Quality Bulletin, a federal regulation that requires peer review for influential scientific information from the US government, he said. The HHS did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about whether this report was commissioned by the agency and if it violated federal regulations. Aaron believes the report would not survive peer review and wondered why a political science report was published by HHS. “It’s actually not even health-related, so I don’t understand why this is related to HHS’s mission,” Aaron said. Craig Konnoth, a professor at the University of Virginia School of Law who coauthored with Aaron a perspective on gender-affirming care policy for the New England Journal of Medicine, agreed. He sees the report as an attempt to undermine mainstream health and science organizations such as the American Psychological Association, American Psychiatric Association, the World Professional Association for Transgender Health, and the American Academy of Pediatrics, all named in the report. “By that standard, any medical recommendation becomes ‘authoritarian’. Any standard set by any licensing board becomes ‘authoritarian’,” Konnoth said. “What we’re seeing is this broadside attack on the scientific establishment more generally, and trans rights are being used as the vehicle to do this.” Colin Wright, an author of the report and a fellow at the conservative thinktank Manhattan Institute, said he believes the study was published by HHS quickly because a draft had been leaked to the public. He said the researchers are planning to release more information, including the numbers from the survey, and they are planning to submit the study to an unnamed journal for publication. “It was kind of a surprise to us that it dropped when it did, and so we didn’t have plans beforehand,” Wright said. “We probably could have tightened the language a little bit more.” Wright disputed that the study was an attempt to link support for trans people and political authoritarianism and violence, though the report itself says: “These findings suggest that gender ideology is associated with LWA [left-wing authoritarianism] and willingness to justify political violence.” Gender ideology was measured by statements such as: “People should be supported in expressing their transgender identity,” and “Parents should support their children’s transgender exploration.” Wright suggested that the study is about the guidance offered by medical organizations and “in many ways geared to make people sort of have a more extreme reaction to it, and to kind of fuel somewhat authoritarian tendencies of trying to silence people” on gender-affirming care. He argued that the guidelines appear to push people toward ideological extremes. “Sort of independently, it increased their willingness, at least correlationally, to their support for political violence,” Wright said. “There’s a lot of ideological content to it.” In an online survey, 1,208 people ranked statements about support for trans people as well as about political ideology and political violence. The political ideology questionnaire essentially measured whether someone was a Democrat, said Meyerowitz-Katz, who added: “I don’t think anyone would think this is a good measure of authoritarianism.” One of the statements was about whether opposition to gay marriage is homophobic; another was a statement about whether the focus on terrorism should shift to the far right. “If you were a rational human being who understood the facts, you would agree with that,” said Meyerowitz-Katz. For instance, approximately 75-80% of deaths from terrorist attacks in the United States come from people on the far right, and rightwing attacks are more lethal than leftwing violence. Similarly, the questions on political violence focused only on political violence against conservative figures or institutions, he said. If they’d included political violence against other actors, “you would almost certainly see the opposite correlation,” making the questionnaire an unreliable predictor of whether someone supports political violence, Meyerowitz-Katz said. It was also difficult to parse these relationships, because the researchers haven’t yet released any numbers from the survey, Meyerowitz-Katz said: “The only thing they report in that paper is correlations.” But they don’t say, for instance, how many respondents supported actions like arson of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) buildings. “This is very silly,” said Meyerowitz-Katz. “They’re producing what I would describe as pseudoscience … It’s a bad, poorly done report.” Trump administration finalizes rule to end federal support for gender-affirming care Read more Konnoth, who studies the link between opposition to LGBT rights and authoritarianism, noted that the report overlooks significant research in the field. “They don’t cite and engage in the data that goes against that thesis,” he said. Typically, HHS publishes issue briefs and synthesized information, but this is an “extremely weird” case of the HHS appearing to adopt a study as its own report, Aaron said. The purpose of the report appears to be an attempt to correlate leftwing people, particularly those who support transgender people, with violence, said Meyerowitz-Katz. “The only possible outcome of this survey was to show a correlation between leftwing beliefs and support for transgender people and ‘political violence’, and so I think that was the aim. I don’t see another possible way to interpret this particular piece of research.” Aaron said it appears to be “aimed to benefit a political group or demonize an opposing group and build political support,” he said. “It kind of builds this fake evidence base for transgender people as a political issue.” HHS is tasked with protecting the health and wellbeing of all Americans, he said, noting: “It’s not happening here.” Aaron compared the report with recent actions on vaccines that depart from the scientific evidence and reshape the vaccine infrastructure – influencing those who make decisions on vaccines and fueling the anti-vaccine political movement. “I think we can draw parallels with this consistent anti-science production of information by the federal government,” he said. Konnoth called it an “attempt to create an alternate scientific narrative” that affects all Americans. “There’s a targeting of these mainstream fundamental organizations that put out research that doesn’t just involve trans rights, but involves broader claims about science,” he said. “If we buy into their attempt to discredit the medical establishment, then we are in deep trouble … It’s life-and-death for massive swathes of the American population.” Explore more on these topics Trump administration Health US healthcare LGBTQ+ rights Transgender US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.ziarulprofit.ro/victoriei-sq.text: Share Tweet The ringleader of the instigators behind the violence in Victoriei Square, along with four other protesters who attacked law enforcement officers, will be brought before the court with a request for a 30-day preventive custody order, as part of a case handled by the Prosecutor’s Office with the Bucharest Court. „On September 15, a protest by livestock farmers took place in Victoriei Square; it soon escalated into widespread violence directed at law enforcement officers and their equipment, resulting in injuries to several gendarmes and damage to vehicles and property. The day before, a 36-year-old man from Bucharest had posted a message on TikTok inciting the public to participate in the demonstration, specifically in a violent manner. Police opened a criminal case for public incitement, which was registered with the Prosecutor’s Office with Sector 4 Court. Given the broader context of the violence, the case was subsequently taken over by the Prosecutor’s Office with the Bucharest Court. Investigations led to the apprehension and identification of five men, including the individual who had incited the public to violence. The five men, aged between 33 and 51, face charges including assault on an official, destruction of property, disturbing public order and peace, and public incitement. They have been formally charged as defendants and were detained overnight. Prosecutors are set to request their preventive arrest for a period of 30 days today,” Diana Calinescu, spokesperson for the Prosecutor’s Office with the Bucharest Court announced on Wednesday. According to judicial sources, the individual who incited people to violence is named Ciprian Pamfile and is a known supporter of Calin Georgescu. He has previously participated in several demonstrations in support of the former presidential candidate; at Tuesday’s protest in Victoriei Square, he appeared shirtless and was subsequently identified and detained by law enforcement. According to the Prosecutor’s Office with the Bucharest Court, investigations conducted so far have established that 10 gendarmes were injured during Tuesday’s protest, with some requiring medical attention, and various pieces of property were destroyed, including a Gendarmerie vehicle, safety barriers, and assets belonging to the STB (Bucharest Public Transport Company). „The protesters are accused of attacking law enforcement officers with metal pipes, clubs, and various objects thrown at them, such as kerbstones, bottles, and metal barriers. They also destroyed the traffic lane dividers belonging to the STB,” the Prosecutor’s Office representative added. Another protester has also been detained in connection with the violence in Victory Square; this individual is being investigated separately in a case handled by the Prosecutor’s Office with Sector 1 Court. O parte dintre liberali consideră că măsurile și direcția politică promovate de acesta au afectat imaginea PNL și riscă să ducă la o prăbușire a partidului. Eșecul era anticipat. https://slguardian.org/europes-far-right.text: The coming contests are unlikely to produce a uniform result. [Representational Illustration] Europe is heading into a year of elections in which Finland, France, Greece, Italy, Poland, Slovakia and Spain will hold presidential or parliamentary contests. The elections involve many of the European Union’s most influential members and come amid internal political turbulence and tensions involving Russia and the United States. Far-right parties are expected to perform strongly across much of the continent, while the established centre-left and centre-right parties are struggling to respond to voters moving towards more radical positions. Turnout, meanwhile, is generally increasing. Germany has provided the immediate warning. Chancellor Friedrich Merz survived three defeats for his Christian Democrats but described the latest result as a catastrophe for Germany. The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) continues to gain support, having moved further towards the extreme right and attracted voters who had previously abandoned the ballot box. Its policies include excluding children without permanent residency from regular schools, establishing citizen patrols and developing closer economic ties with Russia. The Left party is set to run Berlin, while Merz has six months without further regional elections to work with his Social Democratic coalition partners on reforms and economic growth. The coming contests are unlikely to produce a uniform result. Populist parties, most often on the right, will not necessarily take power outright and may not enter government at all. But the source argues that they are increasingly setting the terms of political debate, assisted by social-media activity attributed to the Kremlin and by Donald Trump’s Maga movement. France will provide one of the most closely watched tests. Two rounds of voting in April and May will determine whether Marine Le Pen can become president. Polls currently place her National Rally clearly ahead in first-round voting intentions, although political scientists caution that the electoral cycle means polling will only begin to indicate a clearer direction towards the new year. France’s political centre remains divided over how to respond. If the middle-ground parties fail to unite behind a convincing candidate, the fragmentation could also open a route into the run-off for Jean-Luc Mélenchon. The consequences of a Le Pen victory are disputed. One view is that it could severely damage Nato and EU cohesion, citing Viktor Orban’s record in Hungary, where repeated opposition to or qualification of Nato support for Ukraine complicated efforts to maintain a united position towards Russia. Another possibility is that Le Pen would continue the National Rally’s “de-demonising” strategy, abandoning earlier calls to leave the EU and distancing the party from the Kremlin, following the more pragmatic course associated with Italy’s Giorgia Meloni. Italy, however, is already showing the pressure further to the right. Meloni’s government faces a challenge from the newly launched National Future party, led by General Roberto Vannacci. The party is attracting defectors from the governing coalition and is polling at about 8 per cent, making it Italy’s fourth-largest political force. Vannacci’s platform includes “remigration”, meaning the forced return of immigrants, restrictions on foreign residents, allowing 14-year-olds to enter the workforce and salaries for stay-at-home mothers. Meloni has responded with proposals including bans on burqas and niqabs in schools and limits on foreign students in classes. Spain presents a different political direction. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has opposed Donald Trump, defended immigration and positioned himself prominently among European socialists. Yet four recent regional elections produced poor results for his PSOE, including in former strongholds such as Andalusia and Extremadura. The conservative PP performed comparatively well and the far-right Vox has become a kingmaker. Spain must hold elections by next August, while Sánchez’s previous parliamentary survival depended on fragile agreements with Sumar and Basque and Catalan separatist parties. A recent poll cited in the source puts the far-right separatist Catalan Alliance above 15 per cent. The broader shift is also visible in public attitudes. A 2025 study found that 41 per cent of respondents across 10 European countries agreed that there is a group “trying to replace the native-born population with immigrants”, with 17.5 per cent strongly agreeing. In Portugal, where the far-right Chega was defeated in this year’s presidential election, the unregistered Reconquista movement has already exceeded 5 per cent and campaigns around “population replacement” and remigration. Its leader, Afonso Gonçalves, described Germany’s results as “proof that nationalist and identitarian policies are exactly the kind of policy we need to win elections and save our countries”. Poland will provide another major test next autumn, particularly over Russia and Ukraine. The country has had two centres of power since late 2023, with Donald Tusk leading the government and the far-right Karol Nawrocki holding the presidency. The source argues that electoral arithmetic could enable right-wing and far-right parties to cooperate more effectively than mainstream forces, potentially restoring the Law and Justice party and bringing a return to national-conservative policies and reduced cooperation with Ukraine. The consequences would extend beyond Poland, as Robert Fico in Slovakia and newly elected Czech prime minister Andrej Babiš could sharpen their nationalist positions. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-s-far-righ.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OFpd Following its landslide election win, the far-right AfD has placed itself at the center of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance Advertisement The state parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt is calling for an immediate end to all German financial and military aid to Ukraine. The motion was passed during a special parliamentary session with the votes of the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) which combines left-leaning economic positions with right-wing populist positions on immigration. Both parties are urging Saxony-Anhalt's current state premier Sven Schulze, of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), to advocate in the Bundesrat , Germany's upper house representing the federal states, for peace negotiations with Russia. However, as the federal states have no specific powers in the field of foreign policy, the motion will have no direct impact on Germany's Ukraine policy . Speaking on behalf of the BSW in the state parliament, legislator Claudia Wittig called on the premier to take action: "It is your responsibility to finally use every available avenue to work for peace." The proposal drew sharp criticism from all other parties. "Anyone who demands a ceasefire only from the side that has been attacked is not calling for peace, but for capitulation," said CDU lawmaker Stefan Ruland. What next after far-right AfD win in regional election? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video AfD and BSW bonding over Russia The special session took place against the backdrop of ongoing negotiations over the formation of a new state government in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD emerged as the clear winner of the September 2026 election, securing just under 44% of the vote. However, it fell short of an absolute majority in the state parliament and will need the support of other parties if it is to govern. The BSW, which narrowly secured representation in the state parliament, is the only party willing to hold formal talks with the AfD on forming a government. Because the AfD is classified by the security authorities in the eastern German state as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" party, all other parties have ruled out any cooperation. Observers view the joint motion by the AfD and BSW as a sign of closer and potentially enduring cooperation between two parties rooted in very different ideological traditions. "Their common ground lies in their rejection of the political establishment, their pro-Putin stance, and their criticism of Germany's support for Ukraine," political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber of the Federal University of Applied Administrative Sciences said in an interview with DW. The BSW was founded in 2024 as a breakaway from the socialist Left Party . Its founder, Sahra Wagenknecht , after whom the alliance was originally named, had long been a controversial figure on the German left and advocated far-reaching changes to Germany's economic policy. She was the Left Party's most prominent representative of the so-called "Communist Platform", which maintained close ties to Russia. Over time, however, her socially conservative positions and criticism of Germany's immigration policy came under increasing scrutiny within the party. These growing tensions ultimately led to her departure from the Left Party and the founding of the BSW. The AfD, too, has repeatedly expressed sympathy for Putin's system. Shortly after the start of Russia's war against Ukraine, Björn Höcke , the influential AfD state chairman in Thuringia, described Russia as a "champion of a world of free and sovereign states." Historic parallels The growing rapprochement between the two parties made headlines following a meeting in early October. At the invitation of a far-right publishing house, representatives of the AfD and BSW met in Saxony-Anhalt for what was described as a confidence-building dinner. Also in attendance were controversial figures from both the far right and the dogmatic left. According to their own accounts, participants from both sides explored the possibility of closer cooperation in a cordial atmosphere and in a spirit of mutual trust. Far left? Far right? What is Germany's BSW? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Jürgen Elsässer, the host of the event and editor-in-chief of the right-wing magazine Compact, has for years promoted the idea of a so-called "cross-front" alliance (Querfront) between the far left and the far right in opposition to Germany's political establishment. He has long sought to build bridges between the two camps. Pfahl-Traughber does not regard the cooperation between the AfD and BSW as a "cross-front" alliance: "I am not even sure that the BSW can still be classified as part of the political left." While the party's founder, Wagenknecht, has her roots on the left, she and her allies position themselves on the economic left but the cultural right, the political scientist argued. AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Are both AfD and BSW reactionary? The prominent German historian and author Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk likewise does not consider the BSW as a left-wing party. In an interview with DW, he argued: "The BSW was never left-wing; it was always reactionary." Kowalczuk considers both the AfD and the BSW as threats to democracy: "The BSW and the AfD are two sides of the same coin. Both are mouthpieces for the Kremlin, both pursue similar domestic political objectives, and both seek a comparable anti-democratic transformation of the state into an authoritarian system." Although the recent resolution passed by the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament is unlikely to have any immediate impact on Germany's policy towards Ukraine, Kowalczuk warns of its broader implications: "For now, the AfD and BSW remain isolated, but with positions like these they are appealing to large sections of society, particularly in eastern Germany. The erosion of solidarity with Ukraine will continue and will soon spread to larger segments of both the SPD and the CDU." This article was originally published in German.
